decisions.quote: The high contribution of attitude to the explanation of the variance in intention is also found by Hagger et al. (ibid) in both the exercising and dieting case (exercising = .264, p < .01; dieting = .548, p < .01). The low contribution of subjective norm is also found by Hagger et al. (ibid) in the exercising case (exercising = not given, non-significant) but not in the dieting case where the contribution was high (dieting = .207, p < .01). However, the low contribution of self-efficacy ( = .06, p < .05) to the explanation of the variance in intention is somewhat in contrast with the findings of Hagger et al. (ibid). They found that perceived behavioral control contributed significantly to the explanation of the variance in intention (exercising = .503, p < .0.1; dieting = .221, p < .0.1).
decisions.reason: The supplied full text does not contain the shipped abstract quote, and in the Conclusion the authors give only a qualified summary ('Our preliminary findings thus far supported largely the findings of Hagger et al. (ibid)', line 56; 'The answer to the research question is, therefore, cautiously positive', line 44) specifically because of the self-efficacy discrepancy. In the Discussion (line 40), the authors explicitly mark two tested paths as differing from the original in their own words—noting that the low contribution of subjective norm matches Hagger et al.'s exercising case 'but not in the dieting case where the contribution was high' and that the near-zero contribution of self-efficacy 'is somewhat in contrast with the findings of Hagger et al. (ibid)'—while confirming the remaining relationships. Under the codebook rules for 'mixed', when the paper explicitly marks one or more tested results as contrasting with the original while others agree and does not issue an unqualified overall verdict overriding that contrast, the outcome is 'mixed'.
